citeAs: Krizhevsky, A. (2009). Learning Multiple Layers of Features from Tiny Images. Technical Report.
creator: Alex Krizhevsky
description: CIFAR-100 is a labeled subset of the 80 million tiny images dataset, containing 600 images in each of 100 mutually exclusive classes organized into 20 superclasses of five classes each. Images are 32x32 colour images collected from the web and labeled by paid students. The dataset is intended for object recognition experiments.
name: CIFAR-100
rai:annotatorDemographics: Paid students (no further demographic details provided)
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: Custom in-house labeling task performed by paid students
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Each labeler was given a class and asked to examine all images found with that class as the search term, as well as images found with WordNet hyponyms of the class. Labelers were instructed to reject images not belonging to their assigned class based on criteria: (1) class name should be a likely answer to "What is in this picture?", (2) image should be photo-realistic, (3) image should contain only one prominent instance of the object, (4) object may be partially occluded. Labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour. All labels were personally verified by the authors. Duplicate images were removed using L2 norm comparison.
rai:dataBiases: The source images come with noisy labels (the search term used to find the image) due to the nature of online image search technology. The CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with CIFAR-10 classes, and the 100 classes are organized into 20 superclasses to reflect similarity structure (classes within the same superclass are harder to distinguish).
rai:dataCollection: Images were collected from the 80 million tiny images dataset (assembled by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet using Google, Flickr, and Altavista). Paid students labeled a subset by examining images found under relevant search terms and their WordNet hyponyms, filtering out mislabeled images according to defined criteria.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: 32x32 colour images from the 80 million tiny images dataset, assembled by searching the web using Google, Flickr, and Altavista for images of every non-abstract English noun in WordNet, keeping roughly the first 3000 results per search term.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: Images were downscaled to 32x32 pixels. Perfect duplicates and images with an excessively large portion of white pixels were removed from the source dataset. For the labeled subset, duplicate images were removed by comparing images with the L2 norm using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture re-saved JPEGs.
rai:dataUseCases: Object recognition and image classification experiments. The dataset is intended to provide reliable class labels for benchmarking classification methods on tiny images.
rai:personalSensitiveInformation: The dataset includes a 'people' superclass with subclasses: baby, boy, girl, man, woman — images depicting people categorized by age and gender.

evidence.description: In addition to this dataset, we have collected another set – 600 images in each of 100 classes. This we call the CIFAR-100 dataset. The methodology for collecting this dataset was identical to that for CIFAR-10. The CIFAR-100 classes are mutually exclusive with the CIFAR-10 classes... Furthermore, the CIFAR-100 classes come in 20 superclasses of five classes each.

evidence.rai:dataCollection: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. The labeled subset we collected consists of ten classes of objects with 6000 images in each class... In addition to this dataset, we have collected another set – 600 images in each of 100 classes. This we call the CIFAR-100 dataset. The methodology for collecting this dataset was identical to that for CIFAR-10.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionType: They assembled it by searching the web for images of every non-abstract English noun in the lexical database WordNet. They used several search engines, including Google, Flickr, and Altavista and kept roughly the first 3000 results for each search term.
evidence.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: The labelers were instructed to reject images which did not belong to their assigned class. The criteria for deciding whether an image belongs to a class were as follows: The class name should be high on the list of likely answers to the question "What is in this picture?" The image should be photo-realistic. Labelers were instructed to reject line drawings. The image should contain only one prominent instance of the object to which the class refers.
evidence.rai:annotatorDemographics: We paid students to label a subset of the tiny images dataset. The labelers were paid a fixed sum per hour spent labeling, so there was no incentive to rush through the task.
evidence.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: After collecting all the images for a particular search term, they removed perfect duplicates and images in which an excessively large portion of the pixels were white, as they tended to be synthetic figures rather than natural images... We removed duplicate images from the dataset by comparing images with the L2 norm and using a rejection threshold liberal enough to capture not just perfect duplicates but also re-saved JPEGs and the like.
evidence.rai:dataUseCases: A second problematic aspect of the tiny images dataset is that there are no reliable class labels which makes it hard to use for object recognition experiments. We created two sets of reliable labels... Using these labels, we show that object recognition is significantly improved by pre-training a layer of features on a large set of unlabeled tiny images.
evidence.rai:dataBiases: The search term used to find an image provides it with a rough label, although it is extremely unreliable due to the nature of online image search technology... The idea is that classes within the same superclass are similar and thus harder to distinguish than classes that belong to different superclasses.
evidence.rai:dataCollectionTimeframe: The tiny images dataset on which we based all of our experiments was collected by colleagues at MIT and NYU over the span of six months... All of our experiments were with the CIFAR-10 dataset because the CIFAR-100 was only very recently completed.
